result.topic_en: A two-page spread (printed pp. 192–193). Euler rewrites the interpolation series as an expression in beta-type integrals and interprets it as a curve through given points. He then proposes applying it with circular arcs as abscissae, quoting known sums of partial-fraction series in terms of tangent and sine.
result.transcription:
192
erit per seriem satis concinnam:
$\frac{y}{n\omega} = \frac{p}{n} - \frac{(nn-\omega\omega)q}{n((1-n)^2-\omega^2)} + \frac{(nn-\omega\omega)r}{n((1+n)^2-\omega^2)} - \frac{(nn-\omega\omega)s}{n((2-n)^2-\omega^2)} + \text{etc.}$
siue
$\frac{ny}{n\omega(nn-\omega\omega)} = \frac{p}{nn-\omega\omega} - \frac{q}{(1-n)^2-\omega^2} + \frac{r}{(1+n)^2-\omega^2} - \text{etc.}$
Loco 𝔄 autem formam integralem restituendo, vbi quidem nouam variabilem distinctionis caussa littera $z$ designabo, haec eadem series aequalis est huic expressioni:
$\frac{ny}{(n-\omega)\omega} \cdot \frac{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega} \cdot \int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{n-\omega}}{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-2n}}$
quarum formularum integratio a termino $z=0$ ad $z=1$ extensa est intelligenda.
Corollarium 1.
§. 36. Si ergo breuitatis gratia hanc integralem formam ponamus:
$\frac{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-n-\omega} \cdot \int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{n-\omega}}{\int z^{n+\omega-1}dz(1-z)^{-2n}} = \Delta$
et singulos seriei terminos in binos resoluamus, habebimus:
$\frac{2n\Delta y}{n-\omega} = +\frac{p}{n-\omega} - \frac{q}{1-n-\omega} + \frac{r}{1+n-\omega} - \frac{s}{2-n-\omega} + \frac{t}{2+n-\omega} - \text{etc.}$
$-\frac{p}{n+\omega} + \frac{q}{1-n+\omega} - \frac{r}{1+n+\omega} + \frac{s}{2-n+\omega} - \frac{t}{2+n+\omega} + \text{etc.}$
Corollarium 2.
§. 37. Haec ergo aequatio eiusmodi definit lineam curuam, in qua abscissis
$x = 0,\ n\theta,\ (1-n)\theta,\ (1+n)\theta,\ (2-n)\theta,\ (2+n)\theta,$
respondent applicatae
$y = 0,\ p,\ q,\ r,\ s,\ t,\ \text{etc.}$
iisdem

193
iisdem vero abscissis negatiue sumtis respondeant eaedem applicatae negatiue sumtae. In genere autem hic posita est abscissa $x = \theta\omega$.
Corollarium 3.
§. 38. Quoniam littera $\theta$ ex calculo excessit, eius loco vnitatem scribere licuisset, vt littera $\omega$ ipsam abscissam denotaret. Verum si applicationem ad arcus circulares facere velimus, commodum est litteram $\theta$ in calculo retinere.
Scholion.
§. 39. Vsus huius problematis imprimis cernitur, si vt supra abscissae tanquam arcus circulares spectentur, et abscissae datae ita accipiantur, vt applicatae $p, q, r, s, t$ etc. fiant inter se aequales, siue positiue siue negatiue. Quo igitur his casibus appareat, an series inuenta aliunde summari possit, in subsidium vocentur, quae olim de similibus seriebus sum commentatus; vnde quidem sequentium duarum serierum summae colliguntur:
$\frac{1}{\alpha} - \frac{1}{\beta-\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta+\alpha} - \frac{1}{2\beta-\alpha} + \frac{1}{2\beta+\alpha} - \text{etc.} = \frac{\pi}{\beta\,\mathrm{tang.}\frac{\alpha\pi}{\beta}}$;
$\frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta-\alpha} - \frac{1}{\beta+\alpha} - \frac{1}{2\beta-\alpha} + \frac{1}{2\beta+\alpha} + \text{etc.} = \frac{\pi}{\beta\,\mathrm{sin.}\frac{\alpha\pi}{\beta}}$.
Hinc ergo pro nostro problemate deducimus sequentes summationes quatuor:
I. $\frac{1}{n-\omega} - \frac{1}{1-n+\omega} + \frac{1}{1+n-\omega} - \frac{1}{2-n+\omega} + \frac{1}{2+n-\omega} - \text{etc.} = \frac{\pi}{\mathrm{tang.}(n-\omega)\pi}$;
II. $\frac{1}{n-\omega} + \frac{1}{1-n+\omega} - \frac{1}{1+n-\omega} - \frac{1}{2-n+\omega} + \frac{1}{2+n-\omega} + \text{etc.} = \frac{\pi}{\mathrm{sin.}(n-\omega)\pi}$ [?];
Euleri Opusc. Anal. Tom. I.     Bb     III.

items.quote: haec eadem series aequalis est huic expressioni:
items.english: this same series is equal to the following expression (in terms of integrals from z=0 to z=1).

items.quote: Quo igitur his casibus appareat, an series inuenta aliunde summari possit, in subsidium vocentur, quae olim de similibus seriebus sum commentatus
items.english: So that it may become clear in these cases whether the series found can be summed by other means, let us call to our aid what I once wrote about similar series.
Sum of the alternating partial-fraction series equals pi divided by beta times tan(alpha pi / beta) (quoted from earlier work).
The series with the sign pattern + + − − + + … sums to pi divided by beta times sin(alpha pi / beta) (quoted from earlier work).

items.english: Hence for our problem we deduce the following four summations (only I and II appear on this page; the list continues overleaf).
